name: Jiaoxi Sietian Temple
address: No. 51, Sec. 1, Zhongshan Rd, Jiaoxi Township, Yilan County
description: Most Guan Di temples enshrine a gilded statue, but Jiaoxi Sietian Temple has a 'Silk Guan Gong', an image of Guan Sheng Di Jun built up layer upon layer from silk thread. It is one of the oldest Guan Di temples in northern Taiwan, dedicated to Guan Sheng Di Jun (Guan Gong), and one of the most important centers of faith in Yilan. On the thirteenth day of the first lunar month, the 'Turtle King' rite fills the temple with noise and crowds: worshippers ask Guan Di for a longevity turtle and return a turtle of the same kind the following year. If you want to pray to Guan Gong for your career, for justice, or for peace, this is the stop to make on your way into Yilan.
history: In the summer of 1804, Lin Yingshi, Lin Gurui, Lin Yuzi, Lin Tianlang and others from Zhangzhou brought a branch of Guan Di's incense from the Dongshan Guandi Temple to Taiwan and built a temple in Jiaoxi. Jiaoxi was then the main route for settlers heading into Yilan, and for the Han migrants of Kavalan, struggling to clear new land, Guan Di was the presence they could count on. The temple was expanded and repaired many times from the Qing dynasty through the Japanese era, and a large-scale reconstruction after the founding of the Republic gave it the imposing form it has today. Many Guan Di temples now regard Sietian Temple as their ancestral temple. Its festivals in the first and sixth lunar months are grand occasions, and the temple itself is a page in the story of how the Lanyang Plain was settled.

name: Penghu Tianhou Temple
address: No. 1, Zhengyi St, Magong City, Penghu County
description: Step into Penghu Tianhou Temple and you are standing in the oldest Mazu temple in Taiwan. It was already here before 1604, and documentary research identifies it as Taiwan's first Mazu temple, dedicated to Mazu (the Empress of Heaven). Inside is the oldest stone stele in the Taiwan-Penghu region, inscribed 'Shen Yourong Orders the Red-Haired Barbarian Weimalang and Others to Withdraw', recording how the Ming general Shen Yourong persuaded the Dutch to leave in 1604. The stele is now listed as a national treasure. In 1983 the temple was rated a first-class historic monument (today called a national monument), and its wealth of Qing-dynasty wood carving, stone carving and painted decoration survives intact. If you want to see how Taiwan's earliest temples were built, this is a living textbook.
history: No one knows exactly when the temple was founded, but a standoff at sea fixed its place in history. In 1604, Wijbrand van Waerwijck, a commander of the Dutch East India Company, arrived in Penghu with two ships. Shen Yourong, a Fujian military commander, came with fifty warships to negotiate and talked the Dutch into withdrawing. The episode was carved onto a stone stele, which then lay hidden for more than three hundred years, until a renovation of the temple in 1919 brought it back to light and confirmed Penghu Tianhou Temple as the oldest temple in Taiwan and Penghu. The temple was rebuilt many times through the Ming and Qing dynasties and was renamed Tianhou Temple in 1684, the 23rd year of the Kangxi reign. The buildings still preserve a great deal of Qing craftsmanship.

name: Hualien Shen An Temple
address: No. 118, Cihui 3rd St, Ji'an Township, Hualien County
description: Folk tradition holds that in 1949 (the 38th year of the Republic), the Queen Mother of the West, also called Wangmu Niangniang, Mu Niang or Yaochi Jinmu, manifested and came down to earth at Ji'an in Hualien. Hualien Shen An Temple is the birthplace of the Queen Mother faith in Taiwan. Glittering with gold and regal in style, it is dedicated to Mu Niang and holds a high place among her temples. Shen An Temple and the nearby Cihui Tang share the same origin and later divided into the Yellow-Robe and Green-Robe branches, but as the place where it all began, Shen An Temple still draws countless worshippers back to seek their roots. If you want to reach the source of Mu Niang worship, this is a Hualien stop not to skip.
history: According to legend, in 1949 (the 38th year of the Republic) the Queen Mother of the West manifested around Ji'an in Hualien and watched over the area. Grateful for her answered prayers, the faithful built a temple to enshrine her there, and that was the beginning of Shen An Temple. From Hualien, worship of Mu Niang spread outward. Shen An Temple and Cihui Tang, sharing one source, branched into the Yellow-Robe and Green-Robe systems, and each spread across Taiwan. As the birthplace of the faith, Shen An Temple has been expanded many times and its halls have grown ever grander. Its annual Queen Mother procession, registered as folk cultural heritage in 2013, is still one of Hualien's major yearly events, and it keeps each new generation of worshippers mindful of how Mu Niang came down to earth.

name: Hualien City God Temple
address: No. 169, Chenggong St, Hualien City, Hualien County
description: During the Japanese colonial 'kominka' campaign, many temples across Taiwan were forced to come down, but Hualien City God Temple escaped with one clever move. The temple quietly began enshrining Koxinga (Guoxingye, whose mother, Lady Tagawa, was Japanese, so the colonial authorities saw him as having Japanese blood), and even placed Koxinga's cap on the City God, and so the temple was saved. One of the old temples of Hualien City, it is dedicated to the state-protecting City God (Chenghuang) and has watched a century of change in Hualien. Around the temple you'll find snacks like the famous temple-front black tea, part of a lively neighborhood scene, so it's a good stop whether you come to pay respects to the City God or to eat.
history: Hualien City God Temple was founded during the Japanese colonial era, by one account in 1934 (the 9th year of Showa), and it is the most important center of City God worship in the city. It was modest at first, with the City God as its main deity. As Hualien's population grew after the war, the temple was expanded and renovated several times, which gave it its present appearance.

name: Yilan Sanqing Temple
address: No. 123, Sanqing Rd., Dongshan Township, Yilan County
description: Stand in front of Yilan Sanqing Temple and the whole of Meihua Lake spreads out below you. It is one of the few Taoist temples in Yilan where you can pray and look out over a lake at the same time. The temple is dedicated to the Three Pure Ones (Sanqing Daozu): Yuanshi Tianzun, Lingbao Tianzun and Daode Tianzun, and it is known as the head temple of Taoism in Taiwan. Set between the mountains and the water in quiet surroundings, Sanqing Temple is a well-known Yilan destination for both worship and sightseeing, just right if you want to pray and then take an easy walk.
history: In the 1970s, Sanqing Temple was built on a site beside Meihua Lake. The usual account is that the land was donated by the late county magistrate Chen Jindong. The temple looks out over the lake and the ring of mountains around it, and its main hall enshrines the Three Pure Ones. Every year on the fifteenth day of the second lunar month, the birthday of the Daode Tianzun, the temple holds its most important festival. Over time a full tourism area grew up around the temple, and the Meihua Lake bike path became a popular Yilan outing, making Sanqing one of the few temples where worship and leisure go hand in hand.

name: Ji'an Qingxiu Yuan
address: No. 345-1, Zhongxing Rd, Ji'an Township, Hualien County
description: Walk into Ji'an Qingxiu Yuan and for a moment you may think you are in Japan. This is the only Japanese-style Buddhist temple in Hualien and Taitung listed as cultural heritage. It began as the 'Shingon-shu Yoshino Mission' and is a Hualien County historic monument. In the Japanese era its principal image was Kobo Daishi; after the war it was rededicated to Shakyamuni Buddha and Guanyin Bodhisattva. It has a square 'hogyo-zukuri' roof, a 'Hyakudo Stone' in the courtyard for making wishes, and eighty-eight stone Buddhas modeled on the Shikoku pilgrimage sites, set out quietly one after another in the calm of a Japanese temple. If you are looking for a quiet corner of Hualien where you can slow down, this is a good fit.
history: In 1917 (the 6th year of Taisho), the Japanese priest Kawabata Manji founded this mission in Hualien's Yoshino immigrant village as an outpost of Japanese Shingon Buddhism, and it became a spiritual home for the Japanese settlers of the time. Its principal image was Kobo Daishi, attended by Fudo Myoo and Bishamonten. After the Second World War the Japanese settlers were repatriated and the mission was left to decline. It was later renamed Qingxiu Yuan, rededicated to Shakyamuni Buddha and Guanyin Bodhisattva, and placed under local civilian management. In 1997 it was designated a Hualien County historic monument, and after a full restoration it reopened. Its eighty-eight stone Buddhas copy the 'eighty-eight sacred sites' of Shikoku in Japan, so that worshippers who could not make the long voyage home could still make the pilgrimage close by.

name: Taitung Tianhou Temple
address: No. 222, Sec. 1, Zhonghua Rd, Taitung City, Taitung County
description: Every Lantern Festival, the streets of Taitung put on an astonishing scene: a bare-chested man stands on a palanquin while worshippers hurl strings of firecrackers at him. This is 'Bombing Master Handan', spoken of in the same breath as 'the sky lanterns of the north and the beehive fireworks of the south'. Its home is Taitung Tianhou Temple, dedicated to Mazu (the Empress of Heaven) and the only official temple in eastern Taiwan during the Qing dynasty. The temple keeps the plaque 'Numinous Aid in Pacifying the Rebels' presented by Admiral Zhang Zhaolian, and it was registered as a historic building in 2003. Each year its Lantern Festival 'procession of the gods' and Bombing Master Handan draw thousands upon thousands of people, setting the faith of the 'back mountain' region ablaze.
history: Taitung Tianhou Temple began with the putting down of an uprising. In 1889, the 15th year of the Guangxu reign, Admiral Zhang Zhaolian, grateful to Mazu for protecting him as he quelled a local revolt, proposed building a temple to give thanks. The Guangxu Emperor bestowed a plaque reading 'Numinous, Radiant, Sincere and Protecting', so the temple held the standing of an official temple from the very start. In 1930 an earthquake cracked the building, and the temple was relocated; the new temple on the present site was completed in 1933 and renovated many times into its current form. From a Qing official temple to today's Lantern Festival celebrations, Taitung Tianhou Temple is not only a center of faith but a witness to the story of how Taitung was settled.

name: Matsu Tianhou Temple
address: No. 4-1, Matsu Village, Nangan Township, Lienchiang County
description: Of all the Mazu temples in the world, only this one has, a few steps in front of the shrine in the main hall, the 'spirit cave' where Mazu's body is said to lie. Matsu Tianhou Temple sits beside Matsu Harbor on Nangan, facing the sea. It is the most important center of faith in the Matsu Islands and is dedicated to Mazu (the Empress of Heaven). Legend says that when Mazu's father and brother failed to come back from a fishing trip, Lin Moniang threw herself into the sea to save her father and drowned. Her body drifted to the Matsu inlet on Nangan, and the villagers, moved by her devotion to her father, buried her there and built a temple. Even the name of the Matsu Islands comes from 'Mazu': by the 20th year of the Guangxu reign, a British naval chart was already marking this island as 'Matsu'. The 'Mazu Ascension Festival' on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month is the biggest religious celebration of the year in Matsu.
history: No one knows when Matsu Tianhou Temple was first built, but the story of this place goes back a long way. People were already living around the Matsu inlet on Nangan in the Song dynasty, and Song-era porcelain shards have been dug up here. The gazetteer 'Sanshan Zhi' called Nangan 'Shanggantang'; the name changed to Nangantang only in the Ming and Qing dynasties. The temple has been rebuilt many times. Recorded rebuilds include one supervised by Zhang Yizhou in the 32nd year of the Republic, and a restoration commemorated by a stele inscription in the 52nd year of the Republic. In 2002 (the 91st year of the Republic), the old temple was torn down and rebuilt as a palace-style temple modeled on the Meizhou Mazu ancestral temple, giving it the scale it has today.

name: Kinmen Wudao City God Temple
address: No. 40, Guangqian Rd, Jincheng Township, Kinmen County
description: Every year on the twelfth day of the fourth lunar month, the whole of Kinmen turns out for a great parade, with floats and performance troupes stretching down the streets without end. This is 'Welcoming the City God in Kinmen', listed among 'Taiwan's 100 Religious Sights'. At the center of it all is Wudao City God Temple, dedicated to the City God (Chenghuang) and one of the main centers of faith in Kinmen. The temple has a three-bay, two-hall layout beneath an imposing double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. The day's festivities commemorate a piece of history: in 1680, the Kinmen garrison commander Chen Long moved the seat of government from Kinmen City to Houpu, and the City God moved with it, beginning more than three hundred years of incense in its new home.
history: The temple's roots go back to 1387, when Zhou Dexing, Marquis of Jiangxia, built the walled garrison town at Kinmen City and raised the Gudi City God Temple at the same time. In 1663, the Qing court's coastal evacuation policy left the original City God temple at Houpu in ruins. Then in 1680, Chen Long, the first garrison commander of Kinmen, moved the seat of government to Houpu, and the Gudi City God's incense was divided and brought to Ximen ward in Houpu, laying the foundation of Wudao City God Temple. In 1811, Wen Yingju and others raised more than 2,300 taels of silver to rebuild the temple, and a further expansion in 1994 brought it to its present size. Through all these moves and rebuildings, the bond between the City God and the town of Houpu has lasted more than three hundred years.

name: Hualien Gang Tian Temple
address: No. 15, Ln. 500, Sec. 1, Zhongshan Rd, Hualien City, Hualien County
description: Hualien Gang Tian Temple is the largest Mazu temple in Hualien and Taitung, dedicated to the goddess locals fondly call 'Gang Tian Ma' (Mazu, the Empress of Heaven), and one of the important centers of faith in Hualien City. The grounds are broad, the buildings grand and richly decorated, and the huge double-dragon staircase and the 'spider weaving its web' caisson ceiling make a strong first impression. At its anniversary celebration at the end of each year, the temple holds a grand celebration and procession that brings out the warmth of Hualien's people. If you come to Hualien to worship Mazu, this is the place not to miss.
history: The story of Hualien Gang Tian Temple begins with a statue of Mazu that came across the sea. In the Jiaqing era of the Qing dynasty, an ancestor of a Lin family from Putian brought a statue of Mazu from Meizhou, and at first it was enshrined in the family home. After the war, the statue was entrusted to a Hualien resident surnamed Jian. After the great Hualien earthquake of 1951, worshippers began planning a temple. Construction started on the present site in Hualien City in 1977, on land donated by the wife and children of the then county magistrate Yang Zhongjing, and the temple was completed around 1983, taking the grand form it has today. Today the temple's anniversary celebration at the end of each year brings a large procession; Mazu statues from Baishatun, Beigang and elsewhere have joined it in past years, drawing tens of thousands of worshippers.

name: Tafalong Ancestral Shrine
address: Tafalong Tribe, Guangfu Township, Hualien County
description: In Tafalong, in Guangfu Township, Hualien, lives an Amis community with a long history, one of the oldest and largest Amis settlements. Its ancestral shrine (kakita'an) is the heart of Tafalong's faith and of how its culture is passed down. The shrine's pillars are carved with fine wooden motifs that tell the Amis creation myths and the stories of the ancestors, a precious part of Taiwan's indigenous artistic heritage. The Harvest Festival (Ilisin) in July and August is the most important ceremony of the year: the whole community gathers to sing and dance and honor the ancestral spirits (kawas), giving thanks for their protection of the people and for the gifts of nature. The festival's songs and dances, its feasting and its strict age-grade system show the full shape of Amis society and culture.
history: Tafalong is one of the first large settlements the Amis founded after migrating into the East Rift Valley. In the Amis language, 'Tafalong' means 'white crab', a name said to come from the many white crabs once found in the local streams. The ancestral shrine (kakita'an) is the spiritual center of the community. The original ancestral house was destroyed by Typhoon Winnie in 1958 and was rebuilt in 2006 from drawings left by Chijiiwa Suketaro in the Japanese era; most of the carved wooden pillars that survived are held by the Institute of Ethnology at Academia Sinica. During the Japanese era, Japanese scholars carried out ethnological fieldwork in Tafalong and left valuable written records. In recent years the people of Tafalong have worked hard to revive their culture, restoring the ancestral shrine, singing the old songs again and taking up traditional crafts, and in 2023 they opened the Tafalong Cultural Artifacts Museum, making this old community a model for preserving indigenous culture in Taiwan.

name: Chenggong Tianhou Temple
address: No. 33, Chengguang Rd., Chenggong Township, Taitung County
description: Chenggong Tianhou Temple, also called the Xiaogang Chengguang'ao Tianhou Temple, has more than 150 years of history and is the oldest Mazu temple in Taitung County. In the Qing dynasty, Liu Jin-lai was posted to the "back mountains" of the east as an interpreter-official. Before setting out, he went to Lukang's Tianhou Temple to ask Mazu to travel with him for protection; once he reached Taitung safely, he enshrined her here, and the Mazu faith took root in Taitung. The temple is also a place where peoples met: its founding at first drew opposition from local Indigenous communities, until Pingpu women mediated and the two sides learned to live side by side. On the East Coast, Chengguang'ao is a stop worth making.
history: The temple moved several times before settling in Chengguang'ao, where it became the heart of local faith. When traditional religion was banned under Japanese rule, residents hid the statues in a seaside cave, and the faith survived. In 1949 the temple caught fire. Short on hands and unable to bring painters from the west coast, the rebuilders hired local Pingpu Indigenous people to paint the beams — the first time Indigenous people took part in building a Han temple. Mazu's birthday on the 23rd day of the third lunar month is the busiest day of the year.

name: Yuli Xietian Temple
address: No. 13, Ln. 52, Minsheng St., Yuli Township, Hualien County
description: The temple's greatest treasure is a wooden plaque reading "Guardian of the Back Mountains" (後山保障) — gold regular script on black lacquer, dated the early winter of the seventh year of Guangxu, and now registered as an antiquity by Hualien County. Yuli Xietian Temple is dedicated to Guan Yu (Guansheng Dijun) and is the town's center of faith. In the Qing dynasty Yuli was called Pushige; Qing troops reached it over the Batongguan Trail, and when an epidemic struck they prayed to Guan Yu for protection — the temple grew from that prayer. If you are traveling the East Rift Valley, stop in Yuli to see this old plaque that witnessed the opening of eastern Taiwan.
history: There are two accounts of how the temple began. According to the Yuli Township Office, in 1875 (the first year of Guangxu), Qing general Wu Guangliang led troops over the Batongguan Trail to Pushige — today's Yuli — where an epidemic broke out in camp, and he built a small shrine to pray to Guan Yu. The Hualien County Cultural Affairs Bureau records the folk version: during a great epidemic in the seventh year of Guangxu, Wu prayed to Guan Yu, and after receiving the god's protection he raised a thatched shrine at the camp and inscribed the "Guardian of the Back Mountains" plaque. That plaque is therefore seen as a witness to the temple's founding, and in 2013 Hualien County registered it as an antiquity. The busiest days of the year are Guan Yu's birthday on the 24th day of the sixth lunar month and the Ghost Festival offerings on the 15th day of the seventh lunar month.
